paper_title: LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: LLM-based agents are increasingly capable of generating complex 3D structures, with the potential to reshape how objects are designed and realized in the physical world. Yet, producing elegant geometry is fundamentally different from producing objects that can be built and perform their intended functions. Existing evaluations largely focus on geometric quality while overlooking physical realizability. We introduce LMBuild, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on generating buildable and functional structures. LMBuild represents generated objects as assembled structures comprising part decompositions, joints, materials, and sequences. To support reproducible evaluation, we provide a unified framework consisting of: (1) an interactive environment in which agents can use tools to retrieve, create, and place components to construct objects; (2) a curated benchmark that repurposes established CAD datasets and augments them with knowledge from Wikipedia; and (3) a evaluation framework covering structural soundness, functional affordance, design quality, and physical realization. Evaluations across 30 systems reveal several intriguing findings: (a) Soundness and alignment are no longer the primary bottlenecks for frontier closed-source models, while functional affordance and physical operability remain substantially more challenging; (b) stronger models more effectively create new components, whereas weaker models tend to rely on retrieval; and (c) providing functional specifications substantially improves part completeness, kinematics, and physical operability. These results show that generating real-world structures requires deeper reasoning about functional affordances, mechanics, and designing and creating novel components. We expect LMBuild to provide a foundation for measuring progress and incentivizing research toward agents that generate buildable and functional structures.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly capable of generating complex 3D structures, with the potential to reshape how objects are designed and realized in the physical world. Yet, producing elegant geometry is fundamentally different from producing objects that can actually be built and perform their intended functions. Existing evaluations largely focus on geometric or visual quality while overlooking structural soundness, functional affordances, and physical realizability. We introduce LMBuild, benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on generating buildable and functional structures. LMBuild represents generated objects as assembled structures comprising meaningful part decompositions, joints, materials, and assembly sequences. To support reproducible evaluation, we provide unified framework consisting of: (1) an interactive environment in which agents can use tools to retrieve, create, and place components to construct an object; (2) curated benchmark that repurposes established CAD datasets and augments them with real-world object knowledge from Wikipedia; and (3) fourlevel evaluation framework covering structural soundness, functional affordance, design quality, and physical realization. Evaluations across 30 domain-specific models, open-source LLMs, and frontier APIs reveal several intriguing findings: (a) Structural soundness and visual alignment are no longer the primary bottlenecks for frontier closed-source models, while functional affordance and physical operability remain substantially more challenging; (b) stronger models more effectively exploit part creation to construct structure-specific components, whereas weaker models tend to rely on retrieval and can struggle with the additional flexibility introduced by creation; and (c) providing explicit functional specifications substantially improves functional-part completeness, kinematic correctness, and overall physical operability. These results show that generating real-world structures requires capabilities beyond geometric synthesis, including deeper reasoning about functional affordances, mechanics, and physical constraints, as well as the ability to design and create novel components when existing ones are insufficient. We expect LMBuild to provide foundation for measuring progress and incentivizing research toward agents that generate buildable and functional structures, while helping narrow the gap between open-source communities and frontier labs.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: The recent release of GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026b) has sparked an explosion of discussion around how much LLM-based agents could transform 3D structure generation. Beyond their established capabilities in language and code, LLM-based agents are increasingly able to directly manipulate complex 3D assets and scenes (Hu et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2026a) and translate language-based specifications into parametric or programmatic 3D designs (Li et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Alrashedy et al., 2025). These developments lead us to explore 1 LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures more ambitious possibility: whether LLM agents could reshape not only how structures are digitally designed, but also how they are constructed and realized in the physical world (Kyaw et al., 2025). However, producing visually plausible geometry is fundamentally different from producing an object that can actually be built and function in the real world. structure may appear convincing while remaining invalid, unusable, or impossible to construct. Existing 3D-generation evaluations largely emphasize geometric quality (Poole et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2023), visual consistency (Wang et al., 2023; Maiti et al., 2025; He et al., 2023; Duggal et al., 2025), and semantic alignment (Wu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), while overlooking critical aspects of physical realization. Yet, we still lack systematic way to evaluate whether LLM-based agents can leverage their extensive prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities to generate structures that are not only digitally plausible, but also buildable, functional, and aligned with real-world physical constraints. To this end, we propose LMBuild, first step toward systematically evaluating LLM agents on the generation of buildable and functional structures, while also accommodating domain-specific structure-generation baselines. First, LMBuild provides unified framework (Figure 1) in which LLM agents are equipped with standardized agent harness and can interact seamlessly with 3D environment through set of construction tools, including retrieving components from sub-part pool, creating new parts with arbitrary geometry, placing components at desired poses, and refining structures through inspection and revision. Second, as summarized in Table 1, we select 2,549 highquality reference targets by repurposing existing 3D datasets containing around 368K data, filtering objects by category and model quality, and augmenting them with real-world knowledge extracted from Wikipedia, and further selected 200 objects as the core benchmark dataset for evaluation. This knowledge includes core functional parts, object attributes, joints, and kinematic relationships, which serve as textual anchors for evaluating physically grounded properties. Finally, as shown in Figure 1, we introduce bottom-up evaluation hierarchy covering four dimensions: (1) structural soundness, assessing whether components form valid and stable 3D assemblies; (2) functional affordance, evaluating whether functional parts, joints, and kinematics support the intended object functions; (3) design quality, assessing decomposition, aesthetics, and overall structural design; and (4) physical realization, evaluating whether the structure can be fabricated with appropriate materials and assembly sequences and ultimately operated or used in the physical world. We evaluate 30 systems on LMBuild, including 6 closed-source APIs, 13 open-source LLMs, and 11 domain-specific systems, under diverse evaluation settings. Our results show that: Structural soundness and visual alignment are no longer primary bottlenecks for frontier closedsource models. Most achieve near-perfect soundness and strong design quality, although opensource models still show room for improvement in aesthetics, and fine-grained visual alignment. Functional affordance and physical operability remain the largest capability gaps. All model families struggle with generating complete list of functional parts, correct joints with kinematics, and artifacts that remain operable under simulation-based evaluation. While frontier models can effectively create new components, weaker models rely heavily on retrieval and struggle with the additional reasoning burden introduced by part creation. Enriching prompts with desired attributes and functional requirements can force the model to reason, thus improving functional-part completeness, kinematic correctness, and physical operability. We further show that LMBuild can diagnose failure patterns for open-source LLM agents during structure construction, revealing their gap in part-creation capability as well as persistent challenges in scene-state tracking. Overall, we expect LMBuild to provide foundation for measuring progress and incentivizing research toward agents capable of generating buildable and functional structures.

sections.title: LMBUILD
sections.content: In this section, we describe the three core components of LMBuild: (1) how we construct an interactive environment for evaluating LLM agents and other systems on generating buildable and functional structures ( 2.1); (2) how we repurpose existing datasets to support large-scale LMBuild evaluation and illustrate the interactive generation process with concrete running example ( 2.2); and (3) how we establish hierarchical evaluation framework for the generated structures ( 2.3). 2 LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures LMBuild Framework (Using real example produced by GPT-6 Astra). Given text Figure 1: prompt and conditional image, the builder LLM agent uses tools to inspect and select existing parts, create new parts, and place and adjust components to construct the wheelchair. It then specifies joints, materials, and an assembly sequence to support kinematics and physical-world realization. 2.1 INTERACTIVE GENERATION OF BUILDABLE AND FUNCTIONAL STRUCTURES As shown in Figure 1, LMBuild constructs an interactive environment in which agents are equipped with manually designed harness (detailed in AppendixA.1) and instructed to follow user-provided construction specifications. The agents interact with set of tools (detailed in AppendixA.2) to generate decomposed and buildable structures, determine appropriate joints and materials for individual components, and specify feasible assembly sequence for real-world construction. Baseline Interaction Protocol. LMBuild simulates real-world setting in which users can speak structures into existence (Kyaw et al., 2025). The user provides only target structure label and reference image, without geometric specifications, part-level instructions, or intermediate feedback. The agent then autonomously constructs the object in single interaction round through tool calls (Figure 1), either retrieving components from candidate pool containing at least three times the required number of parts or creating new parts when needed. It selects or creates components, places and adjusts them, and specifies the final pose. For domain-specific systems, we preserve their native input and output protocols rather than introducing unsupported capabilities. When system produces geometry without articulation information, we apply Particulate (Li et al., 2026) to infer part-level articulation, joints, and kinematic constraints for evaluation under LMBuild metrics. Part Retrieval and Creation. The baseline allows agents to either retrieve existing components or create new ones when needed. To isolate the contribution of each mechanism, we additionally evaluate two constrained settings: retrieval-only, where agents must construct the target structure entirely from the provided component pool, and creation-only, where retrieval is disabled and every required component must be generated by the agent. Comparing these settings with the baseline reveals how much agents depend on existing parts versus their ability to design novel components. Multi-Round Iterative Revision. LMBuild also evaluates whether agents can iteratively improve their constructions using feedback. After each round, the environment returns six-view rendering and rule-based diagnostic report covering collisions, disconnected components, stability, joint issues, and missing functional roles, materials, etc. The agent receives this feedback together with 3 LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures Table 1: Statistics of the source datasets repurposed for LMBuild, including original dataset size, objects retained in LMBuild-Core and LMBuild-Full, and average number of Wikipedia-augmented part and affordance annotations obtained. We evaluate budgets of 1, 2, 3 rounds to measure how effectively agents use this feedback for iterative refinement. Prompting with Fine-Grained Descriptions. Beyond the baseline category label and reference image, LMBuild evaluates whether richer task specifications improve structure generation. We augment the prompt with fine-grained descriptions of salient attributes and functional components, providing explicit guidance about what parts should be present and how they should behave or be operated. Comparison with the baseline reveals whether failures stem from insufficient specification of user intent or from limitations in translating detailed requirements into buildable structures. 2.2 REPURPOSING EXISTING DATASETS FOR LMBUILD Evaluating LLM agents for structure generation is substantially more expensive than standard conversational evaluation. Even simple object with fewer than 20 parts can require over 50 interactions in one construction round, with costs increasing further for complex structures and multi-round revision. Exhaustive evaluation over large 3D datasets is therefore impractical, potentially requiring millions turns of LLM generations. From around 368K candidate 3D objects, we therefore construct full benchmark of 2,549 objects and core set of 200 objects through stratified selection from complementary sources, as summarized in Table 1. Rather than matching the frequency distribution of any individual source dataset, our selection is coverage-oriented: we prioritize objects that span diverse construction regimes and capabilities, have verifiable real-world references, and remain tractable for comprehensive evaluation. Due to budget constraints, all experiments in this work are conducted on the core set, while the full benchmark will be made publicly available. Complementary Geometry Sources. No single existing dataset covers the full range of structures and construction regimes targeted by LMBuild. As summarized in Table 1, we therefore combine several complementary sources. BrickNet (Kulits & Schmid, 2026) and BrickComposer (Liu et al., 2026a) provide LEGO-style structures assembled from reusable part inventories with standardized connections. PartNeXt (Wang et al., 2025a) contributes fine-grained part-based objects and static structures, while the Fusion 360 Gallery assembly dataset from JoinABLe (Willis et al., 2022) provides engineering CAD assemblies with explicit part and joint structure. Artiverse (Iliash et al., 2026) contributes physically grounded articulated everyday objects with functional parts and kinematic annotations. Finally, we also collect product-level CAD from 27 opensource hardware projects, with each project publishes complete, buildable product as single assembly file. They span four domains: (1) Robotics and Vehicles, including the ASTRA spinal quadruped (Cominelli, 2025), the Hubert robotic arm (Gildea, 2025), the BiDexHand dexterous hand (Weng, 2025), the OpenROV underwater vehicle (OpenROV, 2020), the Ardumower lawn mower (Ardumower, 2022), the OpenAMR delivery robot (openAMRobot, 2026) and the UPSat CubeSat (Libre Space Foundation, 2017); Consumer Devices, including Ploopy input and audio devices (Ploopy, 2025), the Framework desktop and keyboard (Framework Computer Inc., LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures Figure 2: Left: Generation examples produced by the LMBuild framework. Colors are used only to visually distinguish decomposed components. Right: The generated structures are evaluated using our comprehensive set of evaluation metrics. We briefly illustrate the reference source and general evaluation procedure for each metric; full evaluation details are provided in Appendix A.4. 2026a;b), DIY VR headset (dmcke5, 2025), force-feedback racing pedal (ChrGri, 2026), the OLSK coffee grinder (Ingrassia, 2023), the Shuffle-o-matic card shuffler (DDeGonge, 2022) and Curta mechanical calculator (Wu, 2026); Lab and Medical Instruments, including the OpenRAMAN spectrometer (OpenRAMAN, 2023), biaxial stretcher for live microscopy (Shiwarski et al., 2019), the ShearView rheometer (somexlab, 2026), the NinjaPCR thermal cycler (Hisakawa, 2024), the PolyVent ventilator (Bechard et al., 2024), multi-channel peristaltic pump (Buchhorn et al., 2025) and the OpenAstroTracker star tracker (OpenAstroTech, 2025); and Fabrication Machines and Tools, including the midTbot pen plotter (Dring, 2020), the Precious Plastic recycling machines (Precious Plastic, 2025), the OpenSlider camera slider (Adamslab, 2021), the OLSK 3D scanner and vinyl cutter (Open Lab Starter Kit, 2025a;b), the Voron 2.4 3D printer (VoronDesign, 2025), an automatic wire stripper (Projects with Red, 2023) and the Open Source Ecology CEB press (Open Source Ecology, 2026). Together, these sources span both assembly from reusable part inventories and settings that require structure-specific part creation, and cover broad range of real-world structures, from toys and furniture to complete machines. Data Selection Strategy. Within the combined source pool, we stratify the benchmark data selection along four dimensions. First, we ensure structural and kinematic diversity across six broad families, spanning static load-bearing structures, hinged mechanisms, sliding mechanisms, rotating systems, serial kinematic chains, and multi-joint articulated mechanisms. Second, we prioritize grounded and recognizable objects whose expected components, physical properties, and functional behaviors can be verified from external Wikipedia data; each object category appears at most once in our core set. Third, we maintain difficulty coverage from simple assemblies to complex articulated systems by diversifying the number of parts, and require at least four parts per object. Fourth, we prioritize product-level CAD. These assemblies are the closest proxy for the end goal of LMBuild, building objects that work as real products, but they are orders of magnitude scarcer than part-annotated datasets. We therefore retain every product assembly that passes our screening (a complete single-file assembly, an open license, and recognizable object category). The concrete data selection process and example data are provided in Appendix A.3. 5 LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures

sections.title: 2.3 HIERARCHICAL EVALUATION FRAMEWORK FOR LMBUILD
sections.content: Traditional evaluations of generated structures primarily textbfasize geometric quality or semantic alignment. In contrast, LMBuild evaluates whether generated structure is buildable and functional through hierarchical framework with four complementary dimensions. Structural Soundness (S) assesses whether the generated geometry is physically plausible and structurally stable, avoiding impossible configurations or severe geometric inconsistencies. Functional Affordance (A) evaluates whether the object exhibits the appropriate overall shape, contains the functional parts required by the target category, and specifies joints and kinematics consistent with the intended motion and functionality. Design Quality (D) measures whether the generated structure is appropriately decomposed into meaningful components and whether its overall form and appearance align with the reference structure and human design preferences. Physical Realization (R) evaluates whether the structure can be instantiated in the physical world, including whether it admits feasible robotic assembly sequence, provides sufficient material information for fabrication, and remains operable with respect to its intended functionality. As shown in Figure 2 (Right), these four dimensions are further decomposed into twelve concrete sub-metrics, together with their general corresponding evaluation strategies. To aid presentation, all scores are normalized to common 0100 scale. To avoid overloading the main text with algorithmic details, we provide the complete evaluation criteria and implementation protocols in Appendix A.4, with illustrative examples in Table 4.

sections.title: 3 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 3.1 SETUP Evaluated Systems. We evaluate 30 systems spanning proprietary APIs, open-weight foundation models, and domain-specific generators, covering diverse model families, generations, scales, and architectures. Proprietary systems include GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026b), GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026a), Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026b), Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic, 2026a), Claude Sonnet 5 (Anthropic, 2026c), and Claude Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025). Open-weight models include six Qwen variants across Qwen3, Qwen3-VL, and Qwen3.5 (Yang et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2025; Qwen Team, 2026), spanning 4B35B parameters and both dense and MoE architectures (e.g., 30B-A3B and 35B-A3B), together with GPT-OSS-120B (OpenAI, 2025), Gemma-4-31BIT (Gemma Team et al., 2026), Ministral-3-8B (Mistral AI, 2025), InternVL3.5-8B/38B (Wang et al., 2025c), MiniCPM-V-4.5 (Yu et al., 2025), and ERNIE-4.5-VL-28B-A3B (ERNIE Team, Baidu, 2025). We further compare with domain-specific systems for brick assembly, part-aware generation, and simulation-ready assets, including BrickGPT (Pun et al., 2025a), LegoACE (Xu et al., 2025), PartCrafter (Lin et al., 2025), PartPacker (Tang et al., 2025a), Cube3D and CubePart (Foundation AI Team, Roblox, 2025; Zhu et al., 2026b), and PhysX-Anything (Cao et al., 2025b). Selected part-based generators are additionally augmented with Particulate for joint specification  (Table 3)  . 3.2 MEASURING MODEL CAPABILITIES FOR FUNCTIONAL STRUCTURE GENERATION Overall Observations. As shown in Table 2, state-of-the-art closed-source LLMs achieve the strongest overall performance across most metrics, although several open-source and domainspecific systems remain competitive and occasionally surpass them on individual geometric (e.g., Cube3D(P) on D.2) or realization metrics (e.g., Qwen3.5 models on R.1). Notably, frontier closedsource models, including GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and Claude Fable 5.1, exhibit broadly similar performance across many evaluation dimensions, suggesting that leading model families are converging toward comparable capability level for generating 3D structures. More broadly, overall performance is associated with stronger general reasoning capabilities, while the competitive performance of several domain-specific systems suggests that targeted training and architectural specialization can partially compensate for weaker general reasoning on structure generation. Note that although several systems achieve high performance along individual dimensions, strong performance on single metric does not necessarily translate into high-quality structure overall. Together, these results suggest that generating structurally and visually aligned artifact is substantially easier than producing the functional geometry, complete parts, joint configurations, and kinematics required for the artifact to be fabricated and operate correctly in the physical world. 3.3 STRONG MODELS CREATE, WHILE WEAKER MODELS RETRIEVE We further evaluate LLM agents under three interaction protocols: our baseline setting with both retrieval and part creation, retrieval-only setting, and creation-only setting. As shown in Figure 3, model behavior differs substantially across capability levels. Less capable models degrade sharply when required to create all parts themselves. For example, Qwen3-VL-32B achieves an average score of 61.7 across Soundness and Design metrics under retrieval, but drops to 34.1 under creation-only. Even simply introducing part creation alongside retrieval can reduce performance for weaker models, suggesting that additional design freedom also introduces substantially larger reasoning and decision-making burden. In contrast, frontier models exhibit the opposite trend. They more frequently choose to create their own components when both tools are available, and maintain comparable or even stronger performance when retrieval is removed entirely. For these models, retrieval-only can instead become the more restrictive setting, as the available component pool may constrain their ability to construct geometry tailored to the target structure. This reveals an intriguing capability transition: retrieval helps weaker models by reducing the design space, whereas creation allows stronger models to exploit their generative and structural reasoning capabilities. Part creation therefore appears not merely as an additional tool, but as capability that increasingly becomes beneficial as the underlying model becomes stronger. 3. IMPROVING CAPABILITIES WITH ITERATIVE REVISION AND PROMPTING As shown in Figure 4, we evaluate two common strategies for improving buildable and functional structure generation: (1) allowing models to inspect their outputs, receive error reports, and iteratively revise the structure; and (2) enriching the target description with explicit functional attributes and requirements to encourage deeper reasoning about the underlying structure. Iterative Revision Provides Only Modest Gains. Allowing models to inspect and revise their structures over three rounds leads to steady but limited improvement, with overall gains of only about 2%. Because agents can already interact with and inspect the environment under the baseline protocol, additional revision rounds mainly provide more opportunities to retry rather than addressing the underlying reasoning limitations required for functional structure generation. 8 LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures Figure 4: Average performance change across models from (1) additional revision rounds, (2) explicit attribute requirements, and (3) explicit functional requirements. Revision yields small but consistent gains, while explicit prompts substantially improve functional-part completeness, kinematics, and especially operability. Bars: 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over models; Stars: Wilcoxon signed-rank test over episodes (*p < 0.05, ** < 0.01, *** < 0.001) Explicit Functional Specifications Produce Substantial Improvements. In contrast, enriching minimal prompt with explicit attributes and functional requirements grounded in Wikipedia produces substantially larger gains on the dimensions where current models struggle most. Functionalpart completeness improves by 10.3 points and physical operability by 12.0 points (p < 0.001), with additional improvements in kinematic correctness. These results indicate that substantial fraction of baseline failures can be reduced when functional requirements are made explicit. Current agents therefore appear considerably more reliable at translating specified functional constraints into structure than at inferring all such requirements from minimal object label alone. Implication. Together, these results suggest that improving task specification can be more effective than increasing the revision rounds. promising direction is therefore to develop agents that can more reliably infer, retrieve, or elicit the functional requirements of an object before construction, reducing the need for users to manually provide detailed part-level and kinematic specifications. 3.5 LMBUILD IDENTIFIES FAILURE PATTERNS OF EVALUATED LLMS Open Models Exhibit Part-Creation Gap. Across Part Creation calls, closed-source models succeed on 95.7% of attempts, compared with only 51.7% for open-source models, with Qwen3.527B (89.4%) as the only close exception. Most failures fall into two recurring categories. First, models violate CAD-kernel conventions, such as listing polygon vertices clockwise. Second, models generate invalid program structures by nesting nodes instead of referencing named nodes, using numeric node IDs, or referring to undefined nodes. These errors suggest that much of the creation gap stems from weak adherence to tool-specific conventions and program structure, rather than purely from deficiencies in geometric or spatial reasoning. Open Models Struggle with Scene-State Tracking. Beyond part creation, open-source models frequently lose track of the evolving scene state. They refer to parts that were never placed at rate of 7.2 errors per 100 calls, compared with 0.3 for closed-source models, they often attempt to attach, join, or assign properties to parts whose creation had already failed. They also redundantly add existing entities, including repeatedly placing parts instead of moving them and re-adding existing joints, at 3.2 errors per 100 calls versus 0.5 for closed-source models. Additional interface errors include invalid material names, malformed arguments, exhausted inspection calls, and even invoking part names as tools. Together, these failures reveal broader limitation in maintaining and updating an accurate internal representation of the environment throughout long-horizon construction. sections.title: 4 RELATED WORK
sections.content: 3D Generation with Language Models. Language models increasingly support natural-language 3D creation by generating procedural scripts and scene blueprints (Hu et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2025b) or parametric CAD operation sequences (Khan et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). Visual feedback further enables training and iterative refinement of generated geometry (Huang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b; Alrashedy et al., 2025). These methods connect language understanding with programmatic 3D modeling, but generally focus on producing editable or visually correct geometry rather than structures that can be physically assembled and function as intended. Part-Aware Generation and Physical Assembly. Recent work represents objects as structured collections of parts (Lin et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2025a), predicts joints and articulation (Willis et al., 2022; Li et al., 2026), and incorporates physical attributes such as scale, materials, and motion (Le et al., 2025; Cao et al., 2025a;b). Complementary approaches target stable brick construction, assembly programs, component placement, and robotic execution (Pun et al., 2025b; Kulits & Schmid, 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Goldberg et al., 2025). Together, these works motivate evaluating part structure, physical behavior, and whether the completed object can realize its intended function. Evaluation of 3D Generation. Existing 3D evaluation primarily measures visual quality and text alignment (He et al., 2023), often extended with multimodal judgments of appearance, surface quality, and human preference (Wu et al., 2024; Maiti et al., 2025), or finer-grained geometric and semantic consistency checks (Duggal et al., 2025). For assembled structures, prior work additionally evaluates stability, component selection, placement, and construction success (Pun et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2026a; Goldberg et al., 2025). LMBuild complements these efforts by jointly evaluating soundness, affordance, design, and physical realization across heterogeneous objects using geometric checks, grounded component assessments, simulation-based motion tests, and VLM judgments.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this work, we introduce LMBuild, benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agents on the generation of structured 3D assemblies across four dimensions: structural soundness, functional affordance, design quality, and physical realization. On the LMBuild-Core benchmark, the evaluated systems perform substantially better on structural and visual criteria than on functional-part completeness, kinematic correctness, and simulation-based operability. These results highlight persistent challenges in translating object specifications into coherent components, joints, and assembly plans, as well as in creating task-specific parts when suitable components are unavailable. We hope LMBuild provides reproducible foundation for studying these capabilities and for developing agents that generate increasingly functional and physically plausible structures. Bridging these benchmark results to real-world fabrication and operation will require further validation involving manufacturing constraints, physical assembly, and functional testing. AI USE STATEMENT We used large language models (LLMs) as writing assistants to improve the clarity, grammar, and presentation of the manuscript. We also used AI-based coding agents to assist with evaluationenvironment construction, code refactoring, debugging, code cleaning, and code publishing. All research decisions, experimental designs, implementations, analyses, and reported results were reviewed and verified by the authors. AI tools were not used to determine the scientific conclusions of this work. ETHICS STATEMENT This work aims to support more transparent, accessible, and reproducible evaluation of LLM agents for real-world structure generation. By developing an open evaluation framework, we hope to lower the barriers to systematically assessing model capabilities beyond purely textual benchmarks. In particular, our benchmark emphasizes whether generated structures are not only plausible in appearance but also buildable and functionally valid under real-world constraints. We believe that open LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures evaluation infrastructure can facilitate more rigorous comparison across models, encourage reproducible research, and contribute to the broader open-source AI ecosystem. At the same time, benchmarks can only capture subset of the requirements involved in deploying AI-generated designs in real-world settings. Performance on LMBuild should therefore not be interpreted as sufficient evidence that model is ready for safety-critical engineering, construction, or other physical-world applications without appropriate domain-specific validation and human oversight.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: We provide representative data samples and evaluation materials in the supplementary materials to facilitate inspection and reproduction of our methodology. We will open-source the complete codebase, data, evaluation environment, evaluation scripts, model trajectories from the reported experiments, and all the necessary artifacts required to reproduce our results. We aim to make the full evaluation pipeline transparent and executable so that future work can independently verify our findings, evaluate additional models, and extend LMBuild for constructing more powerful agents.

sections.content: A.1 AGENT HARNESS FOR LMBUILD Overview. LMBuild exposes common interactive assembly environment to heterogeneous model families through lightweight model-specific harness. General-purpose LLM (VLM) agents receive the same environment semantics, task specification, tool definitions, action budgets, and multi-round revision protocol. The harness changes only the mechanism by which observations are delivered and actions are returned: closed-source agents interact with the environment through shell commands, whereas locally served open-source models use an OpenAI-compatible chat interface with text-serialized tool calls. Domain-specific structure-generation systems do not support the common tool interface and are therefore evaluated using their native generation pipelines. This separation allows LMBuild to preserve common task and environment while accommodating substantial differences in model APIs. In particular, the closedand open-source agent settings expose equivalent task information, although image transport, tool-call serialization, and conversation-state management necessarily differ across interfaces. Environment tiers. All general-purpose agents are evaluated in one of three environment specifications. We refer to them as Tier A, Tier B, and Tier for simplicity. Tier permits retrieval and placement of catalog parts only. Tier B, our primary baseline interaction protocol, provides the same catalog while additionally allowing the agent to create new component when no suitable catalog part is available. Tier removes the catalog entirely and requires the agent to create every component before placing it. Except for the corresponding catalog and part-creation instructions, the environment prompt and tool semantics are unchanged across tiers. The environment enforces maximum of 160 tool calls per episode, including at most 6 calls to check, 4 calls to render, and 80 placed parts. Part creation is limited to 30 calls in Tier and 60 calls in Tier C. Both check and render are explicitly described to the agent as metered operations so that they are used for verification rather than unrestricted search. Multi-round interaction. An episode may contain multiple revision rounds. Calling submit ends the current round. When another revision round remains, the environment returns structured diagnostic produced by check together with condition, isometric, front, and side-view images of the current assembly. The agent is asked to inspect this feedback, revise the same scene, and submit again. final submit returns episode done=true. The assembly state is persistent across rounds; therefore, revisions modify the existing object rather than restarting generation. A.1.1 SHARED LMBUILD AGENT PROMPT The following system prompt is shared by all general-purpose LLM/VLM agents. sections.title: The system message is constructed as
sections.content: system prompt(tier) + tool docs(tier) + tool-call protocol, while the user message contains the task text, the condition image when the model supports vision, and the catalog sheet for Tier A/B. Condition images are resized to maximum side length of 1024 pixels, while catalog sheets are resized to maximum side length of 1600 pixels. Because the shared vLLM deployment does not require model-specific native tool parsers, LMBuild uses the following text protocol for all locally served agents: Open-source tool-call protocol Write each tool call as block on its own: <tool_call>{"name": "place_part", "arguments": (cid:44) {"part_id": "P001", "instance_id": "wheel_1", "position": [0, 0, 0.03]}}</tool_call> You may write several blocks in one reply; they run in order and you then see every result. Arguments are strict JSON (double quotes, no comments, no trailing commas). Tool outputs are returned as user messages using the form <tool_result name="TOOL_NAME">{...JSON result...}</tool_result> The parser first searches for explicit <tool call> blocks and then supports small number of model-specific fallback formats, including ERNIE-style <name>/<arguments> outputs, standalone or fenced JSON, and function-like expressions. Automatic repair is deliberately limited to evaluating simple arithmetic expressions in numeric arguments and closing truncated JSON structures. When parsing fails, the model receives the concrete parsing error and is instructed to resend strict-JSON tool call. If model produces no environment action, it is reminded that the interaction contains no human operator and that it should continue through tools or call submit once the object is complete. An episode is terminated after three consecutive responses containing no executable tool call. All locally served models use temperature 0.6 and random seed 0. Model-specific serving modifications are used only when required by the underlying model implementation. A.1.4 DOMAIN-SPECIFIC GENERATION SYSTEMS Domain-specific structure generators are not forced into the LMBuild agent interface when their native architectures do not support iterative tool use. Instead, each system receives the subset of the benchmark condition supported by its original inference pipeline and performs single generation. We retain each methods native representation and prompting procedure rather than adding capabilities unavailable to the original system. For these methods, Tier is operationally identical to Tier because their native generation pipelines do not expose LMBuilds optional create part action. A.2 ENVIRONMENT DETAILS FOR LMBUILD Implementation details of the LMBuild environment. LMBuild is stateful, pure-Python tool environment. Entire episode state coming from LMBuild (placed instances with poses, createdpart programs, joints, assembly sequence, counters and full call trace) is treated as one JSONserialisable dictionary, so the same episode can be driven in-process or from shell, and it can be checkpointed after every round and replayed exactly. World frame and parts All geometry of LMBuild lives in one metric world frame: +Z up, ground plane at = 0, object back facing . Catalog parts are triangle meshes taken from segmented reference assets and stored as glTF. On loading, trimesh converts each mesh with the defined convention and re-centers it on its bounding box. Therefore reduce to exact rigid transforms: translation plus XY Euler rotations, or face-centered alignment of bounding boxes. Part creation The part creation tool accepts declarative CSG program. The program is DAG of at most 96 nodes over box, cylinder, sphere, torus, extrude and revolve primitives. These can 20 LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures Table 3: Comparison of domain-specific structure-generation systems and LLM agents in terms of the information received and produced throughout the construction pipeline. While LLM agents interact seamlessly with LMBuild, domain-specific systems cover only subset. # System Pipeline Input Geometry Parts Roles Joints Materials Sequence PartCrafter-15 PartCrafter-8 PartPacker Generates LEGO Brick Structures Generates LEGO Brick Structures Generates mesh of 15 parts. Generates mesh of 8 parts. The program is compiled with manifold3d (v3.5), which guarantees watertight 2-manifold output. Every created part is therefore valid solid with an exact volume. Parameters are range-checked (0.5 mm3 m), curved primitives are tessellated with 48 segments, and parts that fall apart into disconnected pieces are flagged. Physical feedback All physical feedback comes from one geometry kernel, built on NumPy and SciPy, that is shared with the evaluator. Each placed part is voxelised on 4-mm grid: areaproportional surface sampling, then scipy gives solid occupancy grid. Material Definitions Declared materials are restricted to 23 submaterials in 9 classes. Their densities are medians over 5,510 Artiverse annotations. Rendering Renders are produced out-of-process by headless Blender (bpy 5.2 LTS) worker. The posed scene is exported as GLB, with each part in distinct hue so that parts can be told apart. Each image is rendered with Cycles on the CPU (448 px, 16 samples with denoising, AgX view transform) under three sun lights and above ground plane. The camera has 50 mm lens and autoframing from the designs bounding sphere. Six fixed (azimuth, elevation) viewpoints are available, including one matching the condition images camera. The rendered views are tiled with PIL. The catalog contact sheet is pre-rendered once in the same way. Running restrictions The environment never repairs models action. Invalid calls return explicit error messages and are counted. Budgets limitation include: 160 tool calls per round to restrict unlimited interactions. 6 check calls and 4 render calls per episode; the review returned by submit is free. An episode consists of up to three cumulative rounds (R1-R3). Each submit returns free review (a check plus four views), and the design is checkpointed. Comparability Across System Families LMBuild includes both general-purpose LLM agents and domain-specific structure-generation systems to provide broad view of current capabilities for structured 3D generation. Comparisons should nevertheless be interpreted with respect to the outputs natively supported by each system. General-purpose LLM agents receive the same LMBuild task specification, environment semantics, tool definitions, and interaction budgets, and are evaluated end-to-end across geometry, parts, joints, materials, and assembly sequence. In contrast, domain-specific systems are evaluated using their native inference pipelines and may produce only subset of these outputs, as summarized in Table 3. We therefore report metric as N/A when the information required by that metric lies outside systems native output space, rather than treating the absence of an unsupported output as generation failure. Comparisons between LLM agents and domain-specific systems should consequently be interpreted primarily on their shared applicable metrics, while the complete LMBuild evaluation for LLM agents reflects their ability to solve the full end-to-end construction task. We include domain-specific systems not to imply identical interfaces or capabilities, but to contextualize how specialized generation methods compare with general-purpose agents on the portions of the structure-generation pipeline they support. 21 LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures Information exposed to agents. The environment communicates generic, system-independent construction rules and diagnostic feedback needed to use its tools, while target-specific evaluation sheets and final metric outcomes are not exposed to agents. We view these generic rules as part of the benchmark interface rather than hidden test labels. The functional-prompt experiments intentionally expose additional task requirements and should be interpreted as measuring an agents ability to translate explicit specifications into structures, whereas the baseline also tests whether those requirements can be inferred from category label and reference image. Future work may separately study settings with weaker feedback, hidden interface tolerances, or interactive requirement elicitation. We provide the complete list of 19 tools implemented in the LMBuild environment that models can invoke when constructing structures, together with description of the functionality of each tool. Detailed Description for Tool Set Available in LMBuild Tool: list-parts(query); Function: Lists the parts currently available to the agent, including catalog parts and any parts created by the model, together with their IDs, names, and dimensions. Tool: inspect-part(part-id); Function: watertightness, surface area, and thumbnail path. This tool is unavailable when there is no sub-part pool. Tool: list-materials(); Function: Lists the available construction materials, including their material classes and physical densities. Tool: place-part(part-id, instance-id, position, rotation, role-description); Function: Places selected part into the 3D scene at specified position and optional rotation, and specify its role if possible. It also returns feedback about its bounding box, contacts, collisions, and ground penetration. Tool: set-material(part-id, instance-id); Function: Specify the material of selected part. Tool: move-part(part-id, position, rotation); Function: Moves or rotates an existing part using either an absolute target position or relative translation, while returning updated contact, collision, and ground-penetration information. Tool: attach(instance-id, anchor, target, target-anchor, offset); Function: Aligns an anchor of one part with an anchor of another part or with the ground, enabling structured placement without manually specifying exact coordinates. Tool: measure(part a, part b); 22 LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures Function: Measures the spatial relationship between two parts, including their minimum surface gap, closest points, touching status, and overlap volume. Tool: remove-part(instance-id); Function: Removes placed part from the current structure, together with its associated joints and its entry in the assembly sequence. Tool: set-part-info(instance-id, role, material); Function: Updates the information associated with placed part, such as its functional role and material assignment. Tool: remove-joint(joint-id); Function: Removes an existing joint declaration between two parts. Tool: add-joint(joint-id, type, parent, child, axis, origin); Function: Defines joint relationship between two parts. Supported joint types include fixed, revolute, continuous, prismatic, cylindrical, and ball joints. Tool: set-assembly-sequence(steps); Function: Specifies the intended assembly order of the generated structure, with an optional insertion direction for each assembly step. Tool: create-part(name, program); Function: Creates new custom part from constructive solid geometry program. This tool is available when create new parts is enabled. Tool: get-scene(); Function: Returns the current state of the construction environment, including all placed parts, their poses, bounding boxes, roles, materials, joints, assembly sequence, and remaining interaction budgets. Tool: check(); Function: Use rule-based implementations to check the current structure for potential issues, including collisions, disconnected components, ground contact, stability problems, joint issues, and missing declarations. This tool is metered. Tool: render(view); Function: Generates visual renderings of the current structure from one or more specified viewpoints, allowing the agent to inspect and refine its design. This tool is metered. Tool: submit(); Function: Ends the current interaction round. If additional rounds remain, it returns structural feedback and multiple rendered views before advancing to the next round; after the final round, the task is completed. LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures A.3 DATA SELECTION AND DATA EXAMPLES IN LMBUILD Data Selection Strategy. LMBuild is constructed from heterogeneous pool of approximately 367K raw 3D assets. Because these datasets differ substantially in geometry quality, semantic annotation, part decomposition, and kinematic information, we do not directly sample benchmark objects from the combined pool. Instead, we apply five-stage selection and grounding pipeline designed to ensure that retained objects are structurally valid, sufficiently articulated, semantically identifiable, diverse in their underlying construction, and grounded in independently retrievable realworld knowledge. Candidate Admission and Structural Validity. We first remove assets that are unsuitable for evaluating part-based structure generation. An object is admitted into the candidate catalog only if it contains at least four separately identifiable components, its geometry can be successfully loaded and rendered, and any available joint annotations can be resolved to parts belonging to the same object. These requirements exclude corrupted meshes, effectively monolithic objects, incomplete assemblies, and assets whose kinematic annotations refer to missing or external components. After this initial filtering step, approximately 74.7K objects remain as structurally valid candidates. Source-aware and Diversity-aware Sampling. We next construct manageable candidate subset while preserving structural diversity within each source and semantic category. Because the source datasets differ substantially in their characteristic level of decomposition, we use source-specific part-count ranges rather than imposing single global threshold. We retain Artiverse objects with 460 parts, PartNeXt objects with 540 parts, LEGO assemblies containing 25150 bricks, and Fusion 360 assemblies with 660 components and at least one movable joint. These ranges remove both trivial instances and extremely large assemblies whose complexity is dominated by datasetspecific decomposition rather than meaningful object structure. Within each source-category pair, we then perform diversity-aware sampling instead of random selection. Each candidate object is represented by structural descriptor containing counts of semantic part roles together with counts of moving-part and joint-type combinations. We first select the instance closest to the component-wise median of these descriptors, yielding representative medoid-like example. Subsequent instances are chosen using farthest-point sampling under ℓ1 distance, repeatedly selecting the object that is most dissimilar from the examples already retained. This procedure favors coverage of distinct structural configurations rather than repeatedly selecting near-duplicate instances of the same design. Dataset-specific metadata are additionally used when necessary: LEGO categories are recovered from captions and assemblies are prioritized according to movable connectors such as hinges, axles, and ball joints, whereas Fusion 360 categories are assigned from rendered views using VLM. Semantic Concept Grounding and Visual Verification. Structural validity alone does not guarantee that CAD instance corresponds to well-defined real-world object category. We therefore ground every retained category to both Wikidata and WordNet. For each category name, we retrieve the top Wikidata search candidates and the corresponding WordNet noun synsets. language model is permitted only to select among these retrieved candidates, rather than freely generating an entity identifier. The selected Wikidata item and WordNet synset must denote the general physical object type represented by the category; entities corresponding to brands, named products, artworks, locations, or other non-category concepts are rejected. Categories for which no suitable Wikidata entity can be identified are removed. We additionally verify the category assignment at the individual-instance level. VLM observes two rendered views of each candidate object and determines whether the asset both matches the intended category and represents reasonably complete instance of that object. This step removes fragments, isolated subassemblies, severely incomplete models, and semantically mislabelled examples that may have passed the metadata-based filters. Kinematic Coverage and Core-set Construction. From the grounded candidate pool, we construct the LMBuild-Core benchmark by explicitly covering qualitatively different forms of mechanical organization. Rather than selecting the 50 core tasks solely according to object category frequency, we organize them into six broad kinematic families: (A) static load-bearing structures, (B) hinged mechanisms, (C) sliding mechanisms, (D) rolling or rotating systems, (E) serial kinematic chains, and (F) structures containing many joints attached to common body. These families are intended to expose models to substantially different requirements for connectivity, motion, joint 24 LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures specification, and physical realization. The final 50 core objects span wide range of complexity, from small assemblies containing only four parts to highly decomposed structures containing as many as 417 parts. The remaining selected data form LMBuild-Full, containing 2,349 additional objects from 152 semantic categories. LMBuild-Full may share object categories with LMBuildCore, but it contains no overlapping object instances, allowing the extended set to preserve broader intra-category structural variation without duplicating the tasks used in our primary evaluation. Retrieval-based Real-world Knowledge Grounding. LMBuild further augments each selected object with external knowledge describing its expected components, materials, functional attributes, and mechanisms. Importantly, these annotations are not manually authored from the benchmark designers prior knowledge and are not inferred directly from the CAD geometry. Instead, we construct reproducible evidence bundle from Wikidata, Wikipedia, WordNet, and, only as corroborating source, ConceptNet. For each categorys Wikidata entity, we retrieve structured statements including has part, material, use, uses, powered by, and inverse part of relations. To recover information stated at more general taxonomic level, we additionally traverse up to three levels of subclass of ancestors, retaining at most three ancestors per level and terminating at overly generic concepts such as physical object, product, or equipment. Part and material information may be inherited from these ancestors, but inherited parts are retained only when they have an English Wikipedia article and their own Wikidata entry independently confirms an appropriate part of relation. This conservative inheritance rule reduces the risk of propagating overly broad taxonomic properties to specific object categories. We also pin specific Wikipedia revisions for the target object, identified components, and mechanism-level concepts relevant to the objects kinematic family. For example, hinged structures may retrieve evidence from articles such as Hinge, rotating systems from Wheel or Caster, and articulated mechanisms from Kinematic pair. For identified moving parts, we additionally retrieve relevant Wikipedia article when available. WordNet part and substance meronyms are incorporated as supplementary structured evidence and may be inherited over up to two hypernym levels. Qwen3.527B first proposes candidate claims describing object parts, attributes, subsystems, and kinematic relationships. Every proposed claim must include supporting quotation from the retrieved evidence bundle, and claims whose quoted evidence cannot be matched verbatim to the source text are automatically discarded. This prevents the extraction model from introducing unsupported world knowledge not present in the retrieved sources. second model, Gemma-4-31B, independently evaluates each surviving claim along two dimensions: whether it is supported by the cited evidence and whether it is typical of the general object class rather than an unusual property of particular instance. Core properties and more detailed attributes are assessed separately. When claim fails because its supporting evidence is incomplete or poorly localized, we permit single re-grounding step that retrieves at most three additional sentences from the same evidence bundle; no unrestricted external generation is allowed during this stage. The final annotation therefore retains only claims that can be traced to explicit external evidence and judged to describe characteristic properties of the object category. This pipeline produces the 50-task LMBuild-Core benchmark together with the 2,349-object, 152-category extended set. Each retained knowledge claim remains traceable to its source through either Wikidata entity and statement identifier or pinned Wikipedia page revision and supporting quotation. Evaluation Framework Positioning. Most prior evaluation protocols for generated structures focus primarily on semantic alignment or geometric consistency. In contrast, our framework evaluates buildable structure generation across complementary dimensions of structural soundness, functional affordance, design quality, and physical realization. Importantly, our benchmark spans heterogeneous geometry domains, including LEGO assemblies, mechanical structures, everyday objects, and freely generated meshes, whose representations, part semantics, and physical constraints differ substantially. This cross-domain setting makes many existing domainor representation-specific metrics difficult to apply uniformly, motivating evaluation criteria that can generalize across structure types. Several metrics necessarily introduce heuristic thresholds, tolerances, discretization choices, or weighting coefficients. These hyperparameters were selected based on geometric and physical reasoning, empirical inspection of representative structures, and practical considerations of the evaluation setting. AI tools were additionally consulted during metric development to help examine candidate formulations, identify potential edge cases, and improve the clarity of the evaluation rules; they were not used to determine benchmark outcomes or tune parameters to individual models or results. The resulting hyperparameters should therefore be interpreted as standardized evaluation parameters rather than theoretically optimal values or exact models of real-world physical behavior. All hyperparameters are fixed before benchmark-wide evaluation and applied identically across systems and outputs. We therefore view the proposed metrics as practical, interpretable, and reproducible comparative proxies rather than definitive solutions. Our goal is to provide consistent basis for evaluating heterogeneous generated structures while making the assumptions and limitations of each metric explicit. Interpreting the Scores Where Closed-source API Does Not Lead. For small number of metrics, we observe that another system matches or exceeds GPT-6 Astra. These isolated results, however, should not be interpreted as evidence that the corresponding system is stronger generalpurpose builder. Each metric captures only one aspect of generated structure, and high performance on particular dimension may arise from properties enforced by the systems representation, from producing simpler structures, or from optimizing visual appearance at the expense of functionality. We therefore examine these cases individually and explain why such scores can be misleading when interpreted in isolation. Soundness of Brick Generators. BrickGPT and LegoACE achieve the strongest results on the connectivityand collision-related Soundness metrics, outperforming all API-based systems on these dimensions. This advantage is largely explained by their representations and decoding procedures rather than by broader design capability. Both systems generate structures on discrete stud lattice, and BrickGPT further rejects placements that would collide with existing bricks and LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures rolls back unstable construction steps. As result, connectivity and collision avoidance are strongly enforced by construction. However, the same systems perform substantially worse on metrics that assess whether the generated structure corresponds to the requested object and contains the appropriate functional components. Their Design and Affordance scores remain comparatively low, indicating that structure can be physically coherent without faithfully realizing the intended object or its functionality. These results therefore illustrate that high Soundness is necessary, but not sufficient, for successful structure generation, and it is not suprising that several systems could outperform the best LLM-based solutions. Soundness of Part-based Mesh Generators. related effect appears among part-based mesh generators. Particulate and Cube3D+CubePart achieve strong scores on selected Soundness metrics because their generation procedures naturally encourage geometric compatibility between parts. Particulate first generates complete mesh and subsequently segments it into components, meaning that the resulting parts inherit shared surface and are unlikely to interpenetrate. CubePart similarly generates parts within common object volume, which encourages contact between adjacent components. This geometric consistency, however, does not necessarily imply structural robustness. For example, PartCrafter performs substantially worse on load-bearing stability, suggesting that its components are not always connected in mechanically meaningful ways. These results distinguish geometric compatibility from structural reasoning: parts may fit together spatially without being designed to support one another under physical constraints. Soundness and realization of simpler designs. Several open and smaller general-purpose models also match or outperform GPT-6 Astra on selected Soundness and Realization metrics, particularly those related to supported connections, assembly executability, and material plausibility. key factor is that these systems tend to produce considerably smaller assemblies. For example, Qwen3.5-27B and GPT-OSS-120B generate designs with substantially fewer parts than GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5. This difference directly affects metrics such as S.1, R.1, and R.2, all of which become easier to satisfy as assembly complexity decreases. Fewer parts imply fewer interfaces at which unsupported or incorrect connections can occur, shorter assembly sequences reduce the number of ordering dependencies, and smaller set of generic components simplifies material assignment. The corresponding tradeoff appears on metrics that evaluate completeness, decomposition quality, and functional structure. Systems that produce simpler assemblies tend to omit required components and mechanisms more frequently, resulting in lower Affordance and Designfidelity scores. This pattern suggests that strong performance on local structural or realization criteria can partly reflect reduced design complexity rather than stronger end-to-end generation capability. Moreover, many failures captured by these metrics are locally repairable: geometric gap can often be closed, fastener added, or material reassigned without changing the overall design. In contrast, missing mechanism, incomplete decomposition, or incorrect functional structure usually requires more fundamental redesign. We therefore interpret Soundness and low-level Realization metrics as important necessary conditions, while Affordance, Design fidelity, and Operability provide stronger evidence of whether model can generate the object as complete functional system. Effective-part generation of Cube3D+CubePart. Cube3D+CubePart performs notably better than other mesh-based generators on effective-part generation and also surpasses several open generalpurpose models. This result should be interpreted in the context of its input representation. CubePart receives an explicit part schema, and in our evaluation protocol this schema corresponds to the set of components required by the task. The system therefore begins with substantial information about which parts should be present, rather than having to infer the decomposition entirely from the conditioning input. Our metric still requires those components to occupy appropriate spatial locations, so the system does not receive full credit merely for reproducing the supplied labels. Nevertheless, part of its advantage reflects access to the expected component inventory. Its simulation results further show that the presence of correctly named parts does not necessarily translate into functional articulation, as the generated components rarely produce meaningful motion. Aesthetic quality of mesh generators. Mesh-based generators show different form of specialization on the aesthetic metric. Cube3D and related systems produce smooth, coherent, and visually refined surfaces and consequently perform very well on reference-free aesthetic evaluation. This behavior is consistent with their training on large collections of 3D assets, where generating polished and watertight surface is central objective. This distinction is reflected in the gap between reference-free aesthetics and reference-conditioned Design fidelity. Conversely, image-to-3D reconstruction methods such as PartPacker achieve stronger visual fidelity to the target object but still lack the articulation and functional decomposition required for high Affordance and Operability. Aesthetic quality should therefore be interpreted together with fidelity and functionality rather than as an independent indicator of overall design capability. Material generation of PhysX-Anything. PhysX-Anything is distinctive among the specialized generators because it explicitly predicts material for each generated component. As result, it achieves meaningful performance on material plausibility, unlike most domain-specific baselines. This result demonstrates useful capability, but it should not be conflated with end-to-end product realizability. The system still produces relatively coarse part decompositions, and its generated objects exhibit almost no successful functional operation in simulation. Material plausibility therefore captures one aspect of realization quality, but does not by itself indicate that the generated structure is complete, mechanically functional, or manufacturable as coherent product. Overall interpretation. Taken together, these cases reveal three recurring reasons why specialized or open system may match or exceed the strongest closed-source API on an individual metric. First, some properties are guaranteed or strongly encouraged by the output representation itself, as in lattice-based brick generation or mesh segmentation. Second, some metrics become easier to satisfy when system generates smaller and less complex assemblies. Third, systems optimized for visual quality can perform well on appearance-based criteria without necessarily reproducing the correct object structure or functionality. These observations motivate interpreting LMBuild as multidimensional benchmark rather than comparing systems through isolated metric maxima. Soundness, material plausibility, and aesthetic quality capture important properties of generated structure, but none alone establishes that the system has identified the correct components, organized them into the intended design, and produced the required functionality. Across the metrics that more directly require these capabilities, including effective-part generation, functional decomposition, reference fidelity, and operabilitym the closed-source APIs remain strongest overall. The consistency of the level-level results across object sub-samples further suggests that these differences reflect persistent variation in end to end model capability rather than advantages tied to small set of objects or individual metrics.
