All systems produce design for every task, indicating that their primary limitations are functional rather than procedural. Physical defects do occur, but they are generally secondary: between 6.5% and 21% of generated designs contain at least one disconnected part, while 3%16.5% contain interpenetrating parts, with Claude Haiku 4.5 representing notable outlier at 38% and 38.5%, respectively. Most of these defects are small gaps or overlaps, particularly on LEGO and product-CAD objects, and could plausibly be corrected through local geometric adjustments. The more consequential failures arise from incomplete functional decomposition. A.3 is the weakest Affordance metric across these systems, with an average score of 37.9. Among failed motion targets, 57% fail because the required moving component, such as lid, steering link, or handle, is never generated; further 17% include the relevant part but lack joint capable of moving it. The remaining failures are associated with incorrect joint type, axis, range, or offset. similar pattern appears in A.2: in 54.5%68.5% of designs, at least half of the required components are missing or incorrectly positioned, with many omissions corresponding to internal parts that are not directly visible from the exterior. These decomposition failures propagate directly to functional execution. R.3, which evaluates each declared capability according to its weakest required element, averages only 18.3 across the six systems. Nearly every design omits at least one component referenced by its functional description, such as timer, thermal sensor, or lever. As result, no evaluated capability succeeds at all on roughly 30%40% of tasks, increasing to 51% for Claude Haiku 4.5. Assembly planning introduces an additional source of error: between 48% and 68% of generated assembly sequences are not fully executable. The first failure is often floating component, such as main body placed before the legs or supports required to hold it, even when the final geometry could in principle be assembled under different ordering. In contrast, low-level tool interaction is rarely the limiting factor. Only 2%7% of create part calls fail, and the models typically recover from these failures within the same episode. Performance also varies systematically across object sources. Product-level CAD and Fusion 360 objects are the most difficult, with 81% and 73% of designs, respectively, missing or misplacing required components, compared with 48% for Artiverse furniture 62 LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures and appliances. Qualitative examples reinforce the same pattern: Claude Opus 5 can generate toaster with recognizable bread slot while omitting the lever, timer, thermal sensor, and ejection mechanism; it can produce toilet with plausible seat hinge but no lid or flush handle; and GPT6 Astra can generate an off-road vehicle with rotating wheels while failing to provide articulated steering links. Taken together, these results suggest that current frontier models are comparatively effective at producing recognizable external geometry, but remain substantially weaker at recovering the internal component structure, articulation, and mechanisms that make an object function. This gap is precisely what the Affordance and Realization levels of LMBuild are intended to capture. A.6 LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK Evaluation scope and interpretation. LMBuild is designed as standardized framework for comparing generated structures, rather than as certification procedure for real-world engineering readiness. Its metrics operationalize buildability and functionality through reproducible geometric, semantic, kinematic, and simulation-based tests. These tests provide substantially stronger evidence than visual plausibility alone, but they do not establish that generated artifact can be fabricated, assembled, or operated safely in every physical setting. In particular, the current evaluation does not model manufacturing tolerances, fastener strength, elastic deformation, fracture, fatigue, tool access, wiring or fluid routing, actuator limits, or sustained loading. LMBuild scores should therefore be interpreted as measures of performance under fixed benchmark criteria and as comparative evidence of physical and functional plausibility, not as proof of deployability or safety. Approximate physical models. Several evaluation components necessarily use simplified physical assumptions. Stability focuses on tipping; assembly feasibility uses discretized insertion paths and intermediate-support checks; and operability uses rigid-body simulation with standardized density, friction, collision geometry, and actuation parameters. These choices make evaluation deterministic and comparable across heterogeneous structures, while isolating geometric and kinematic feasibility from uncertainty in inferred physical properties. Nevertheless, different parameterizations or higherfidelity models may change individual scores, especially for structures whose operation depends on deformable components, material-specific behavior, or complex contact. Future work should study metric sensitivity and ranking stability under alternative thresholds and simulation parameters, and validate representative subset through physical fabrication, robotic assembly, or expert mechanical assessment. Benchmark coverage. The experiments in this paper use the 50-object LMBuild-Core split. This split is deliberately coverage-oriented: it spans multiple structural families, articulation regimes, construction paradigms, and difficulty levels rather than reproducing the empirical frequency distribution of any one source dataset. Consequently, the reported results characterize performance across the selected construction regimes but should not be interpreted as population-level estimates over all real-world objects. The 2,399-object LMBuild-Full split is intended to support broader evaluation, including category-level analysis, rare mechanisms, and more difficult productscale assemblies. Extending evaluation to the full split and to additional domains such as compliant mechanisms, electronics, and fluid-powered systems is an important direction. Automated evaluation and human calibration. Design Quality combines deterministic measurements with two VLM judges calibrated against ratings from four human annotators. On held-out designs, the resulting metrics preserve system-level human rankings well, while item-level correlations and human-human agreement show that individual designs remain inherently more ambiguous. The present calibration covers limited set of objects and systems and may not capture every valid design style or decomposition strategy. In addition, Wikipedia-derived capability sheets provide an auditable source of real-world knowledge but may omit uncommon components or alternative realizations. Future versions should broaden the annotator and system pool, include domain experts where appropriate, report uncertainty for agreement statistics, and continue expanding accepted component synonyms, material alternatives, and functional realizations. System comparability and statistical uncertainty. General-purpose agents receive the same task specification, environment semantics, tool definitions, and budgets, but provider-specific execution interfaces and modality support necessarily differ. Domain-specific systems additionally retain their native inputs and outputs and are therefore comparable only on shared applicable metrics. Unless otherwise stated, the current results use one final generation trajectory per model-task pair. Confidence intervals obtained by resampling benchmark objects quantify variation across tasks, but not within-model stochasticity across repeated generations. Future evaluation should include repeated 63 LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures runs where computationally feasible, standardized native tool-calling interfaces, and reporting of both task-level and run-level uncertainty. Outlook. Beyond scaling models and tool budgets, future work should improve the knowledge, skills, and creative physical reasoning that models bring to structure generation. First, models could internalize reusable construction knowledge, including geometric constraints, assembly rules, component affordances, and functional properties, rather than rediscovering them at inference time. Recent work on textual and multimodal policy internalization suggests that such structured knowledge can be incorporated more directly into model behavior (Liu et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026). Similar methods could provide stronger priors for joints, interfaces, load-bearing structures, clearances, and other recurring physical constraints. Second, building agents could acquire reusable procedural skills through exploration and interaction. Work on environment exploration, recursive self-improvement, and reasoning skills shows that agents can discover and retain useful strategies from experience (Liu et al., 2026c; Zhu et al., 2026a; Zhao et al., 2026). In LMBuild, agents could similarly explore alternative construction strategies, learn from failed checks or simulations, and accumulate reusable skills for creating parts, joints, and mechanisms. Third, future systems should support more creative physical construction, including inventing functional parts, repurposing components, and refining designs through multi-turn interaction. Recent work highlights the difficulty of affordance-based creative reasoning in multimodal models (Qian et al., 2026b;a). Combining such reasoning with iterative tool use, execution feedback, and code-based construction interfaces could enable agents to propose, test, and revise increasingly functional designs (Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024). complementary direction is to close the loop between digital generation and physical fabrication. Future extensions could incorporate additive-manufacturing constraints such as minimum feature size, wall thickness, overhangs, tolerances, material choice, and build volume, and evaluate whether generated structures can be successfully printed, assembled, and operated. Physical validation would enable direct measurement of print success, dimensional accuracy, assembly feasibility, structural integrity, and functional performance, while supporting sim-to-real calibration of LMBuilds evaluation metrics. Beyond 3D printing, future work could consider additional manufacturing processes, richer material and contact mechanics, fasteners, compliant components, and electrical or fluid routing. Expanding evaluation to LMBuild-Full, repeated generations, and evaluator-sensitivity analysis would further improve coverage and reliability. Ultimately, LMBuild could serve not only as benchmark for buildable generation, but also as an environment for studying how agents acquire the knowledge, skills, and creative physical intelligence required to construct functional real-world artifacts.
